newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Cyprus gambit holds real risks for West.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Cyprus gambit holds real risks for West.

text.p: Turkey's threats to attack Greek Cypriot forces over a fresh military build-up on the divided island are part of a deliberate scare tactic that could easily spin out of control, analysts said.

Fueling the danger is Ankara's new-found distance from its traditional Western partners, which are calling on all sides to exercise restraint in their row over a Greek Cypriot decision to purchase ground-to-air missile batteries.
Turkey last week threatened several times to knock out Russian-made S-300 missiles if Greek Cypriot authorities deploy them as planned on the south of the split Mediterranean island.
"If it came to it, I think the Turks would probably shoot," one European diplomat said. "They have become numb to criticism to a certain extent."
Some 30,000 Turkish troops still occupy the north of Cyprus, visible from the Turkish coast and regarded by many Turks as a mere extension of the Anatolian land mass.
The fact that the Greek Cypriot missiles have sufficient range to strike planes in Turkish airpace brings the matter closer to home.
"There is the feeling here of a real threat to national interests," a NATO diplomat said.

Already, the United States is pressuring its close ally Ankara to lower the temperature, terming the threats "irresponsible." It has also sent Carey Cavenaugh, head of the the State Department office for southern European affairs, to the region for talks.
A Turkish spokesman dismissed the public U.S. criticism as beyond "the limits of diplomatic courtesy."
The United Nations and Ankara's Western allies have plenty of time, however, to step in as the rocket system is not due on Cyprus for more than a year.
"It is still at the bluff stage and there is a long way to go, but we are taking this very seriously," the NATO diplomat said.

Domestic commentators say the bellicose rhetoric -- Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller has said any such missiles would be "hit" -- is largely a gambit to scare the West into convincing the Greek Cypriots not to go ahead with the arms purchase.

"The crisis...is positive in that it focuses the world's attention on the Greek Cypriot armament and contributes to a solution to the problem in a manner desired by us," columnist Mensur Akgun wrote at the weekend in the daily Yeni Yuzyil.
Turkey appears to be gambling the West will not risk key projects like NATO and EU enlargements which would be in endangered by a Turkish strike on Cyprus.
A conflict would set Ankara and Athens, formally NATO allies but bitter foes, further against each other and put in doubt EU membership talks Cyprus is likely to hold next year.
But old certainties no longer hold, raising the stakes in the latest showdown.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, has worried Western capitals with friendly overtures towards Iran and radical Arab states.

The veteran Erbakan has long taken a tough line against the Greek Cypriots. He was second-in-charge of the government that ordered troops to invade Cyprus in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup that Ankara says threatened the island's Turkish Cypriot minority.
His deputy today, Ciller, is an outspoken nationalist.
"They are both hawks on Cyprus," the Western diplomat said. "It is not inconceivable that (Turkey) would carry out the threats."
Turkey's influence abroad has quietly slipped since the early 1990s, leaving the Cyprus issue -- known as "The National Cause" -- as one of the few areas Ankara feels sure of itself.
The end of the Cold War deprived Turkey of the strategic value it had for decades as the only NATO member, along with Norway, bordering the Soviet Union.
Ankara has seen much of eastern Europe, including its Greek Cypriot foes, leapfrog it in the queue for European Union membership despite Turkey applying to join a full 10 years ago.
An ailing economy and a poor human rights record have kept Turkey distanced from the EU and a year-old customs union with Europe has shown few benefits for Turks.
A turbulent domestic scene, meanwhile, suggests Turkish officials are whipping up the Cyprus affair to divert attention from trouble at home.

Erbakan's coalition has been embroiled in a security scandal that has left it little time to attack annual inflation of 80 percent and end the Kurdish conflict that has cost more than 21,000 lives in the last 12 years.
"I fear this (Cyprus) crisis could be an effort to draw a curtain over domestic problems...and deflect attention abroad," columnist Sami Kohen said.
